title: Lab-grown meat: Order up!
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss lab-grown (in vitro, cultured) meat: PETA's one-million-dollar prize for commercially viable cultured meat, the key researchers Gabor Forgacs (Modern Meadows, University of Missouri) and Mark Post (Maastricht University, Netherlands), Winston Churchill's 1931 prediction, Morris Benjaminson's 2002 goldfish-muscle experiment, cost estimates per pound versus conventional beef, the hurdles of taste, texture, fat, blood and vessels, the environmental benefits (greenhouse gases, land, water, grain efficiency), rising global meat demand, and a listener mail email from Colin about the Independent Study mentorship program. The episode closes with a teaser for a future factory farming episode.

entities.name: People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts greet listeners, joke about the previous episode on condoms, and introduce lab-grown meat as a possible future food source.

segments.title: PETA prize and key researchers
segments.summary: PETA offered a one-million-dollar reward for commercially viable in vitro meat by June 2012, which was not met. The hosts describe the first in vitro hamburger taste test and the two leading researchers, Gabor Forgacs of the University of Missouri (Modern Meadows) and Mark Post of Maastricht University in the Netherlands, and Forgacs's 2011 TED talk tasting.

segments.title: Churchill's prediction and the goldfish experiment
segments.summary: Winston Churchill predicted growing chicken parts separately. Morris Benjaminson grew goldfish muscle cells in fetal bovine serum, gaining about fourteen percent more mass, and initially imagined the product for astronauts.

segments.title: Animal rights support, 2008 Norway conference and cost
segments.summary: Animal rights groups supported the idea. A 2008 Norway conference study estimated production at about five thousand dollars a ton. The hosts estimate a retail price near eleven dollars a pound after a markup, and compare it to Kobe beef and lobster pricing.

segments.title: Technical hurdles: tissue, texture and bioprinting
segments.summary: The Dutch team uses cow stem cells to grow small muscle pieces that resemble calamari and taste bland because they lack fat, blood and veins. Modern Meadows proposes using three D printing to layer bio-ink. Growing healthy cells needs nutrients, hormones and minerals. Post's first burger was expected to cost about 330,000 dollars.

segments.title: Costs, first products and environmental benefits
segments.summary: Forgacs sees lab-grown meat as a niche product and expects leather first. Early food products may be ingredients like meatballs. Cited benefits include about 78 percent fewer greenhouse gases, much less land and water, and better feed-to-meat efficiency. Global meat demand is expected to double in 40 years.

segments.title: Health benefits, public acceptance and taste
segments.summary: Jason Matheny of New Harvest says cultured meat could be healthier, with easier pathogen control and controllable fat content. The hosts discuss whether they would eat it, the public's squeamishness, and naming.

segments.title: Listener mail from Colin about mentorship
segments.summary: Colin, a high school senior in Texas, writes that the podcast has helped with essays and projects in his Independent Study mentorship program. The hosts plan a future factory farming episode.

segments.title: Sign-off and resources
segments.summary: Hosts point listeners to the HowStuffWorks innovations channel and social media for contact.
